status: Final nine historical source duties reviewed through prepared reuse/task protocols; no further new claim proposed. Full labels are source-fit authoring designs, not observed pupil success or default-branch acceptance.

contact-programme.role: All four actual early encounter packets and explicitly later Métis outcome; retain their sources, periods, uncertainty and independent knowledge checks.

new-france-programme.role: Actual royal administration, parish/religious/education/care and landholding repertoire; no modern-government backdating.

early-organisation.role: Complete previously reviewed fixed Haudenosaunee and Classic Thule knowledge protocol; attribution and archaeological/analogy limits retained, not a direct early Inuit constitution.

current-institutions.role: Retain the complete current Canadian institutional repertoire and exact source-specific authority/representation distinctions; one current MNO comparison is not whole-claim mastery.

port-royal-history.locator: Hard Times for the Colonists, main body paragraphs after 1607 departure through 1614 return
facts: An English expedition burned the Habitation in 1613 while its inhabitants were away. On returning in 1614, Poutrincourt found the destruction and his son/companions living with Mi’kmaq.
This gives an actual European-conflict consequence for the settlement and a documented Indigenous–French support relationship; it does not establish all Mi’kmaq opinion or a present title outcome.
port-royal-history.limits: Both 1613 and 1614 precede 1713; do not confuse the later 1939 reconstruction with original buildings. No first-settlement superlative or invented eyewitness speech.

wendat-2013.locator: Nation-authored memorandum,22 April 2013, printed5–7 historical sections and printed3 statement of purpose
facts: The Nation links its historical Sillery presence, the 1651 seigneury/Jesuit guardianship arrangement and later dispossession to its objection that the 2013 heritage conservation proposal omitted its historic/current presence and rights.
Use this as the Nation’s attributed historical-and-contemporary argument, not a pupil legal/title determination or a claim the exact2013 proposal is still pending today.
wendat-2013.limits: Do not backdate the 1760 treaty, nineteenth-century displacement or 2013 population to pre-1713. Historical continuity and source arguments are distinct from modern legal adjudication.

wendat-current.locator: Current main Nation-authored community, diplomacy, territory and language sections, checked2026-11-11
facts: The Nation describes its continuing identity, territory relationship, diplomacy and contemporary community institutions. Compare this current self-description with the dated 2013 memorandum without assuming every historic/current claim has been legally adjudicated.
wendat-current.limits: Exclude placeholder art text and broad constitutional-influence claims. Current elected roles are not evidence of seventeenth-century offices.

facts: The Nation’s attributed account describes formerly warring founding Nations choosing peaceful shared decisions and chiefs/Clan Mothers working for community well-being. Its proposed founding date is an estimate.
onondaga.limits: No exact date is required; do not turn a traditional account into an eyewitness transcript or a universal system for all Indigenous peoples.

confederacy.locator: About the Haudenosaunee Confederacy main body
facts: The Confederacy states that its exact founding date is unknown and distinguishes a Nation’s own council/internal affairs from shared Grand Council concerns.
confederacy.limits: Continuing traditional relationships and present policies are not automatically backdated. Do not infer that cooperation means conflict never occurred.

mno-current.role: Already reviewed current Chartered Community Council relationships in the Canadian institutional programme; distinguish current representation from the separate dated emergence findings.

actions: Explain a supported useful exchange and a serious harmful consequence for named parties in the actual cases. Identify who was affected and why the effect mattered to community life, safety, movement or continuing relationships.

Contrast immediate exchanges with later consequences such as coercion, epidemic loss, trade-network change or community formation. Attribute accounts and avoid a universal friendly-contact or inevitable-extinction story.
consequences.success: Actual positive/negative consequences and their significance are explained; calling everything good/bad or equating benefit with consent is insufficient.

actions: Use the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence packet to explain distinct benefits: European access to furs, transport/route knowledge and markets, and First Nations access to particular desired goods through existing relationships. Identify who supplied the knowledge and materials.

Explain a supported benefit without claiming all parties benefited equally, every offered item was useful or benefits removed harmful/coercive outcomes. Later Métis interpreting/kinship/community contributions retain their actual chronology.
benefits.success: A supported different-party benefit relationship, not a list of objects or invented motive; knowledge and agency remain explicit.

actions: Trace the explicitly dated earlier trade/family conditions, later Great Lakes/Mattawa collective development and contemporary Métis representation. Explain how a historical relationship can matter to current community identity/representation, without making ancestry-only or individual-rights conclusions.

Compare the Nation’s actual 1651/Sillery historical account and its dated 2013 conservation objection with current self-description. Explain whose perspective connects earlier colonial administration/land relationships to a heritage/territory issue; distinguish an attributed claim, continuing identity and a legal finding.
Consider a new account that claims a colonial landholding map proves nobody else had rights. Explain why neither that map nor the current community source alone settles all modern title questions.
present-connections.success: Specific source-supported historical-to-present connections, with early/later/current periods and authority/representation limits explicit; not a generic respect slogan.

actions: Identify the studied Wendat in the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence trade network, Mi’kmaq in Acadia/Port-Royal and Qikiqtani Inuit in the Baffin encounter, using a verified locator and the actual pre-1713 dates. Explain that these are selected distinct peoples, not a complete all-Nations inventory.

Describe supported characteristics from the actual cases: the Museum identifies the Wendat as an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people and trade intermediaries; the Port-Royal account documents Mi’kmaq local survival/route knowledge and named leadership; QIA documents the Inuit food/skin exchange and retained oral records. Separate these source-backed characteristics from universal gender, belief or modern-government assumptions.
Keep later Métis collective emergence separate rather than falsely insert it into the list of pre-1713 communities.
nations-characteristics.success: Actual identification and meaningful characteristics of selected Nations/communities; names alone, all-peoples stereotypes or a backdated Mattawa community do not suffice.

actions: Explain the attributed Haudenosaunee founding-peace relationship among distinct Nations, including peaceful shared decisions rather than an exact independently proved founding year. Retain the whole two-case organisation claim and source distinctions.

Explicitly record that the reviewed packet does not yet establish a chronologically supported pre-European First Nations–Inuit interaction. Geographic overlap or a later traditional account is not enough to infer a particular early trade or conflict.
pre-european-interactions.remainingCondition: A source-supported pre-European First Nations–Inuit interaction is not yet verified. This is a bounded resource/chronology condition, not evidence no interactions occurred or a reason to invent a new topic.

actions: Retrieve and compare the whole learned Haudenosaunee founding/decision relationship and qualified Classic Thule harvesting/leadership/resource-sharing model. Explain a supported difference and reason connected to the actual collective purpose and organisation; identify the model/analogy limit rather than present a witnessed early constitution.

Compare those with actual New France appointed crown/governor/intendant and religious/landholding relationships. Explain how learned institutional traditions and different collective purposes support particular differences, without assuming ethnicity/climate determines every person’s behaviour or one status implies human worth.
Give a new attributed role/decision account: use its actual facts to compare, and leave an unsupported authority or belief inference unknown.
community-differences.success: Differences among selected Indigenous arrangements and between Indigenous/European arrangements, with supported reasons and source/period limits. All fixed prior knowledge claims are retained rather than narrowed to one convenient role.

actions: Explain the actual 1613 English attack’s destruction of the French Habitation and the reported 1614 situation of French survivors living with Mi’kmaq. Identify the European imperial conflict, its settlement consequence and the documented effect on Indigenous–European relationships.

Use the earlier trade/alliance packet to explain how rival European commercial/military relationships could affect particular Indigenous partners. Do not reduce every seventeenth-century conflict to one cause or imply a Nation disappeared.
Compare a new short attributed case of rival colonising powers: which effect is documented, and which effect on a local community would require more evidence?
european-conflict-effects.success: Significant effects for actual Indigenous/community relationships and future-Canada settlement history; no exhaustive European-war or battle inventory is imported.

actions: Produce one coherent explanation connecting earlier Indigenous networks and trade/alliance relationships, European competing enterprises and Indigenous–European encounters. Compare actual short effects with the separately dated longer-term relationship/community outcomes.

Use the 1701 negotiation and its earlier conflict context for interactions among Indigenous Nations, the 1613/14 Port-Royal case for European rivalry and consequences, and the trade/Qikiqtani packets for different Indigenous–European exchanges and harms. Explain source limits rather than make every interaction one universal pattern.
integrated-consequences.success: All three interaction categories and short/longer consequences are actually used; the specific protocols remain required, not replaced by an overall link.
